articles.excerpt: Android development involves more than writing code and building applications. Developers also need tools to inspect APK files, test compatibility, troubleshoot installation problems, and verify appli…
articles.body: Android development involves more than writing code and building applications. Developers also need tools to inspect APK files, test compatibility, troubleshoot installation problems, and verify application security. An APK, or Android Package Kit, is the file format used to distribute and install Android applications, containing the compiled code, resources, and components needed for installation. Many utilities can help developers work with APK files, but choosing the right tools matters — unverified software can introduce security risks, produce misleading results, or damage project files.

articles.title: Hasty Paste links need a retention policy before reachability becomes exposure
articles.excerpt: Hasty Paste links need a retention policy before reachability becomes exposure Hasty Paste is a self-hosted pastebin with a browser interface and a REST API. The official project documentation describ…
articles.body: Hasty Paste links need a retention policy before reachability becomes exposure Hasty Paste is a self-hosted pastebin with a browser interface and a REST API. The official project documentation describes fast text sharing and optional expiring pastes. Those features make the service useful for operational notes, logs and incident handoffs. They also turn a paste URL into a bearer-like secret: anyone who has the link may be able to read the content unless the deployment adds a separate access control. The service is designed to be reachable. A public landing page or API route is not automatically a finding. The security question is whether the person creating a paste understands who can read it, how long it remains available and whether the server stores a second copy after deletion.

articles.body: First, what a week Can we take a second for the week we just had? Microsoft 365 went down for the better part of a day, with Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot all dark across the world, and a few days later Bell Canada said an "agentic" attacker had made off with enterprise customer data. Our tools going quiet, and AI agents turning up on the wrong side of a breach, all in one stretch. One quick note, so we stay accurate. The two are not the same story. Microsoft said the outage was a network change gone wrong, not a cyberattack. The Bell breach was real, and the "agentic" part is the bit worth sitting with, because attackers are now pointing AI at the job of breaking in. So no, there is no single magic version to be on. articles.body: On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and…

articles.title: Studying Cancer Cells in Microgravity
articles.excerpt: This Nov. 19, 2026, image shows gastric microtumors grown within an Encapsulates biochip. The Encapsulate-1 investigation studies patient-derived tumor samples aboard the International Space Station t…
articles.body: Encapsulate Inc. This Nov. 19, 2026, image shows gastric microtumors grown within an Encapsulates biochip. The Encapsulate-1 investigation studies patient-derived tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to better understand how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. The results could help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments. Orbiting more than 200 miles (320 km) above Earth, the space station is a powerhouse of cutting-edge science that is unlocking discoveries not possible on Earth. Image credit: Encapsulate Inc.

articles.title: Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance
articles.excerpt: These strange geological features may offer clues to the Red Planet's watery past.
articles.body: NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.
